sections.title: Where you are right now
sections.body: Right now, you’ve built a pretty solid base. You’re confident your teen is not using substances, you rarely see them in situations where substances are around, and you stay in close touch with where they are and who they’re with. Your teen talks openly with you about stress and emotions, takes responsibility for mistakes, and you describe disagreements as calm and easy to work through. At home you already have clear rules, consistent rewards and consequences, and a strong routine with sleep, school, meals, and activities. You and the other parent or guardian are on the same page, with a written plan you both know you can act on. You feel supported by school and community adults, and you’re already in contact with a therapist. For guidance, consider posting questions in the Sustaining Recovery discussion group. In Admin Spaces, under Treatment Providers, you can find a listing of treatment providers & therapists who endorse and support the ASAP program. This is a “pay attention early” moment more than a crisis — a chance to keep sharpening what’s already going well so you notice any change quickly.

sections.title: Your first three priorities
items: Pause before reacting, even when things are going smoothly. You already feel confident and rarely doubt yourself, which is a strength. The next step is to keep a habit of taking one or two slow breaths, or a quick mental check-in, before you respond when your teen brings you something stressful or surprising. That way, what your teen sees is your steadiness, not any brief spike of irritation, worry, or impulse to fix things fast. When rules are broken, keep pairing clear consequences with clear rewards, and deliver both in that same calm tone.

Keep the adult team tight and current. You and the other parent or guardian are already aligned on rules, tone, and a written plan. Use that strength: briefly review the plan together this week, confirm what each of you will do if you start noticing earlier warning signs, and agree on the same rewards and consequences you’ll both stick to. That way, if something shifts, you’re not scrambling; you’re following the playbook you already agreed on, and your teen sees one steady message from the adults at home.

Strengthen your own support so you can keep showing up calmly over time. You’re already connected to school, community supports, and a therapist, which gives you a good base. For guidance, consider posting questions in the Sustaining Recovery discussion group. In Admin Spaces, under Treatment Providers, you can find a listing of treatment providers & therapists who endorse and support the ASAP program. Also reach out to the Monitoring and Intervention discussion group to hear how other parents with “nothing urgent, but paying attention” situations keep watch without becoming anxious or intrusive. The more grounded you feel, the easier it is to keep conversations with your teen steady and collaborative.

recommendations.title: Parent Emotional Regulation
recommendations.headline: Keep your steadiness as your main tool
recommendations.body: You’re already mostly calm, confident, and not feeling worn down by this, which is ideal at this stage. Now the work is to protect that steadiness so it’s there if things change. When something about your teen’s behaviour or social life catches your attention, make it a habit to pause: notice your first reaction, take a breath, and decide if this is a moment to ask a curious question now or wait until later. Use short, matter-of-fact language and keep your tone even, especially when you’re setting rewards and consequences. If you notice yourself getting reactive, step away for a few minutes and write down what you actually want to say before you say it. If you start seeing more secrecy, unexplained schedule changes, or signs of early use this week, the next step is to bring that to the Monitoring and Intervention discussion group and ask how other parents would respond in your shoes.

recommendations.title: Know what you are looking at
recommendations.headline: Sharpen your eye for early warning signs
recommendations.body: Because things are going fairly well, the most powerful move right now is to get very clear on what real early warning signs look like, instead of guessing or worrying in the abstract. You already feel confident your home discourages substance use and that you’d know what to say if something changed. Back that up with concrete knowledge about small shifts in sleep, mood, school, money, social circles, or online behaviour that often show up first. This lets you notice a pattern in days, not months, and gives you specific things to watch for without hovering. Watch Auxiliary Workshop "Early Warning Signs – Identifying Substance Use Before It Becomes a Problem" and jot down two or three signs that would mean, for you, "time to act." If you see any of those specific signs appear or build over this week, the next step is to schedule time with your teen to review house rules and your written plan together.

sections.title: What to avoid
items: Do not assume that because things look good now, they will automatically stay that way. You have strong routines and a clear plan; avoid drifting into autopilot where you stop noticing new friends, schedule changes, or mood shifts. Stay observant without becoming suspicious.

Do not turn every small concern into a heavy talk. Your teen is open with you; over-responding to minor issues can make them less willing to share. When something small comes up, start with a curious question and keep the tone light unless you see a real pattern.

Do not search your child's room, backpack, or phone confrontationally or in the heat of an argument. Conduct any search of your child's room, backpack, or phone privately and without your child present. Leave the room as you found it and document anything relevant. If you ever choose to do this, tie it back later to safety and your existing rules, not to catching them out.

Do not let rewards quietly fade while only consequences stay active. You already keep consequences consistent; make sure you are just as consistent about noticing and rewarding honesty, responsibility, and healthy choices, so your teen feels you see more than just problems.

Do not sideline your own support because things feel calm. You’re connected to school staff, community supports, and a therapist already. For guidance, consider posting questions in the Sustaining Recovery discussion group. In Admin Spaces, under Treatment Providers, you can find a listing of treatment providers & therapists who endorse and support the ASAP program. Keeping those channels active now makes it much easier to respond quickly if something shifts.

sections.title: Your first 72 hours
sections.body:
Day 1:
• Take 5–10 minutes alone to check in with yourself: what, specifically, are you watching for, and what is actually going well? Name both.
• Review your written plan and house rules, including how rewards and consequences work. Make sure you feel comfortable delivering them calmly.
• Notice one example today of your teen handling stress, responsibility, or a rule well, and name it out loud to them in a simple, neutral way.

Day 2:
• Touch base briefly with the other parent or guardian and confirm you’re still aligned on rules, tone, and how you’ll respond if you see early warning signs.
• Watch Auxiliary Workshop "Early Warning Signs – Identifying Substance Use Before It Becomes a Problem" and skim reliable information on early signs for the substances most common in your area.
• For guidance, consider posting questions in the Sustaining Recovery discussion group. In Admin Spaces, under Treatment Providers, you can find a listing of treatment providers & therapists who endorse and support the ASAP program.
• Reach out to the Monitoring and Intervention discussion group to hear how other parents in similar “early watch” situations keep an eye on things.

Day 3:
• Choose a low-stress moment (driving, cooking, walking) to talk with your teen. Keep it brief.
• Say that you’ve been learning more about substances because you care about safety, and ask how things are going at school and with friends.
• Re-state your basic expectations about no use, along with the rewards for honesty and healthy choices, and the consequences you’ll follow if rules are broken. Keep the tone collaborative: you and your teen on the same side against substances, not against each other.

sections.title: Days 4 to 7
sections.body:
Over the next several days, your job is to keep the tone steady and follow through on what you’ve already laid out.

If your teen brushed off the Day 3 conversation, denied any issues, or acted irritated, treat that as information, not a crisis. Stay calm, keep routines solid, and watch for specific early signs you identified from the workshop: changes in sleep, school performance, social patterns, or honesty. If you notice nothing new, keep the subject light and occasional, and continue to reward responsible behaviour and open conversations.

If you do see concerning small shifts, meet briefly with the other parent or guardian to agree which concrete step from your written plan you will now put in place. That might be tightening certain curfews, requiring check-ins, or adjusting access to money or devices, always with clear rewards for showing responsibility again. If your teen escalates or argues about these changes, hold the agreed boundary calmly and remind them it’s about safety, not punishment.

Stay in touch with your therapist during this week as needed. For guidance, consider posting questions in the Sustaining Recovery discussion group. In Admin Spaces, under Treatment Providers, you can find a listing of treatment providers & therapists who endorse and support the ASAP program. Keep using the Monitoring and Intervention discussion group to pressure-test your next steps before you act.

workshops.title: Early Warning Signs – Identifying Substance Use Before It Becomes a Problem
workshops.whyThisFamily: You’re confident your teen is not using substances, and you already have strong rules and routines. Auxiliary Workshop "Early Warning Signs – Identifying Substance Use Before It Becomes a Problem" will help you translate that general confidence into a clear list of specific signs to watch for, so you can respond quickly if anything starts to shift.

sections.title: Match the Intervention to the Risk
sections.body: The level of intervention should always match the level of risk. Too much intervention can be as counterproductive as too little. As concerns increase, your response should increase with them; as risk decreases, your response can adjust accordingly. The goal is not to use the strongest intervention available—it is to use the level of intervention that best matches what is actually happening with your child.

sections.title: Taking Care of Yourself
sections.body: Taking care of yourself is not a luxury—it’s a necessity. Whether you need some quiet time, a good workout, or the support of counseling, make space for what helps you stay grounded. When you care for yourself, you will be better able to show up strong, present, and healthy for you and your family.

sections.title: Where this can go
sections.body:
You’ve done something many parents never quite do: you paid attention early, built clear rules, stayed closely informed about your teen’s life, and even put a written plan in place with the other parent or guardian before things got messy. That groundwork matters.

From here, the goal isn’t to become suspicious; it’s to stay observant and informed, so if substances ever do show up around your teen, you both face that problem together. The substance is the problem, not your teen. Your calm, consistent follow-through and willingness to listen are already helping your teen talk openly about stress and own mistakes.

You don’t have to do this in your own head. The Monitoring and Intervention discussion group exists for exactly this in-between space, where nothing is on fire but you want to stay sharp. Over time, children and circumstances change, so it’s worth coming back to your plan and these supports every so often and adjusting as your teen grows.
